ai.literal: Thinking of [it] the intoxication, and seeing [it] the delight, to liquor is not there, to love is there.
ai.translation: To feel intoxicated just by thinking of it, and to feel delighted just by seeing it—these belong not to liquor, but only to love.
ai.modern: நினைத்த உடனே களிப்பு அடைதலும், நேரில் கண்ட உடனே மகிழ்ச்சி அடைதலும் ஆகிய இவ்விரண்டும் மதுவுக்கு இல்லை; ஆனால் காமத்திற்கு உண்டு.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the effects of liquor and love. While liquor can only intoxicate after it is consumed, love has the unique power to intoxicate the mind the very moment one thinks of the beloved. Similarly, merely seeing the beloved brings immediate delight. The poet contrasts these two experiences to show that the joy of love is far superior and more immediate than any physical stimulant.

words.gloss: even to the size of a millet seed
even to the size of a palmyra tree

ai.literal: Even to the size of a millet seed, not sulking is necessary, when love, even to the size of a palmyra tree, comes abundantly.
ai.translation: One must avoid feigned anger even to the tiny measure of a millet seed, when love arises in abundance, swelling to the vast size of a palmyra tree.
ai.modern: பனைமரம் போன்ற பெரிய அளவில் காம உணர்வு நிறைந்து வரும்போது, தினை அளவு கூட ஊடல் கொள்ளாமல் இருக்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the urgency of lovers who are eager to reunite. The speaker explains that when love and desire swell to a massive size, symbolized by the tall palmyra tree, one must not indulge in even the tiniest bit of feigned anger, symbolized by the tiny millet seed. Any delay caused by sulking, however brief or small, becomes unbearable when passion is overwhelming. The contrast between the tiny millet seed and the large palmyra tree beautifully illustrates the disproportionate pain that even a minor lovers' tiff can cause when desire is at its peak.

words.gloss: the lord of the maritime tract

ai.literal: Without cherishing, even if he does only what he desires, without seeing the lord of the maritime tract, they do not rest, the eyes.
ai.translation: Even if my lord acts only as he pleases without cherishing me, my eyes will not rest unless they see him.
ai.modern: தலைவன் என்னை மதிக்காமல் தன் விருப்பப்படியே செய்தாலும், அவனைக் காணாமல் என் கண்கள் அமைதியடையா.
ai.explanation: In this verse, the heroine describes her uncontrollable longing to her companion. Even when her husband, the lord of the maritime tract (koṇkaṉ), neglects her feelings (pēṇātu) and acts solely according to his own desires (peṭpavē), she cannot remain angry. Her eyes (kaṇ) refuse to find rest or be satisfied (amaiyala) unless they can behold him (kāṇātu). The word 'amaiyala' combines 'amai' (to rest or be content) and the negative plural suffix 'ala', perfectly capturing how her eyes rebel against her own resolve to stay away.

ai.literal: Towards sulking I went indeed, O friend! That having forgotten, towards union went my heart.
ai.translation: O friend! I went with the intention of sulking, but my heart, completely forgetting that resolve, rushed towards union.
ai.modern: தோழியே! நான் அவரிடம் ஊடல் கொள்ளவே சென்றேன்; ஆனால், என் நெஞ்சம் அதை மறந்துவிட்டு அவரோடு கூடுவதற்குச் சென்றுவிட்டது.
ai.explanation: The heroine shares her helplessness with her companion after meeting her lover. She had firmly resolved to show feigned anger (ஊடல்) to prolong the sweet pleasure of reconciliation. However, the moment she saw him, her heart completely forgot that intention and rushed to embrace him. The contrast between 'ஊடற்கண்' (towards sulking) and 'கூடற்கண்' (towards union) highlights the conflict between her conscious mind and her uncontrollable feelings. Ultimately, her heart acted independently of her will, surrendering to love.

ai.literal: When painting, like the eyes indeed that do not see the painting rod, I do not see the faults of my husband when I see him.
ai.translation: Just like the eyes that cannot see the painting-rod while collyrium is being applied to them, I cannot see any of my husband's faults when he is before me.
ai.modern: கண்களுக்கு மை தீட்டும்போது அந்த மையைத் தீட்டும் கோலைத் தன் கண்கள் காணாதது போல, என் கணவனை நான் நேரில் காணும்போது அவனுடைய தவறுகள் எதையும் நான் காண்பதில்லை.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine describes her inability to hold a grudge or remember her husband's faults once he is in her presence. She compares this to the act of applying collyrium to the eyes. When the painting-rod ('kōl') comes extremely close to the eyes to beautify them, the eyes themselves cannot see the rod. Similarly, when her beloved husband ('koṇkaṉ') is close to her, his physical presence and love completely overwhelm her, making it impossible for her to see or remember any of his flaws ('paḻi') that she had previously intended to confront him about.

ai.literal: When seeing, I do not see faults that are; when not seeing, I do not see other than faults.
ai.translation: When I look at my lover, I do not see any of his faults; but when I do not see him, I see nothing but his faults.
ai.modern: நான் என் காதலரைப் பார்க்கும்போது அவருடைய தவறுகளைக் காண்பதில்லை; அவரைப் பார்க்காதபோதோ, அவருடைய தவறுகளைத் தவிர வேறு எதையும் காண்பதில்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet beautifully captures the psychological state of a longing heroine. When she is in the presence of her lover, her immense love blinds her to all his flaws, and she sees him as perfect. However, when he is away, her longing and grievance make her dwell only on his mistakes, and she cannot recall any of his good qualities. The contrast between 'seeing' and 'not seeing' highlights how love alters perception based on presence and absence.

ai.literal: Like those who leap into the water knowing it will carry them away, what is the use of sulking, knowing it will prove false?
ai.translation: Like those who plunge into a rushing flood knowing it will sweep them away, what is the use of my sulking when I know it will dissolve the moment we meet?
ai.modern: வெள்ளம் அடித்துச் செல்லும் என்று தெரிந்தே அதில் குதிப்பவர்களைப் போல, என் ஊடல் அவரிடம் தோற்றுப்போகும் என்று தெரிந்தும் நான் ஊடுவதால் என்ன பயன்?
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine compares her feigned anger or sulking to jumping into a swift river. Just as a person leaping into a flood knows they cannot resist the current and will be swept away, she knows her resolve to remain angry will instantly dissolve when her lover approaches. The word 'uyttal' refers to being carried away by the water, and 'poyttal' refers to her sulking proving false or failing to hold up. Thus, she questions the utility ('eṉ') of sulking when she knows she will inevitably yield to love.

ai.literal: Even if you do disgraceful and painful things, to those who are intoxicated, like liquor indeed is, O deceiver, your chest.
ai.translation: O deceiver! Even if you do disgraceful and painful things to me, your chest is like liquor to those who are already intoxicated by it.
ai.modern: கள்வனே! நீ அவமானப்படத்தக்க துன்பங்களைச் செய்தாலும், உன்னால் மயங்கியவர்களுக்கு உன்னுடைய மார்பு மதுவைப் போன்றதே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine addresses her lover as a deceiver or rogue (கள்வ) because of his hurtful behavior. She explains that even when he causes her shameful distress (இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும்), she cannot stay away from him. His chest or embrace (மார்பு) acts like liquor (கள்) to an addict (களித்தார்க்கு). Just as a drunkard craves more alcohol despite the harm it causes, she yearns for his embrace despite the pain he inflicts.

ai.literal: Even than a flower, softer is love; few its delicate nature attain.
ai.translation: Love is more delicate than even a flower; yet, only a few are able to truly attain and experience its subtle, tender nature.
ai.modern: காமம் மலரை விடவும் மென்மையானது; அதன் நுட்பமான தன்மையை அடைந்து இன்புறுபவர் சிலரே ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the extreme sensitivity of love by comparing it to a flower. While a flower is known for its softness, love is described as being even more delicate and easily bruised by the slightest insensitivity. The word 'cevvi' refers to this peak, tender state of love that requires perfect timing and gentle handling. The poet observes that only a rare few possess the deep understanding and emotional refinement needed to experience love in its truest, most delicate form.

ai.literal: With her eyes having sulked indeed, she became confused, [for] embracing, more than me, she herself eagerness having experienced.
ai.translation: She feigned anger only with her eyes and immediately lost her resolve; for she herself was far more eager for our embrace than I was.
ai.modern: அவள் தன் கண்களால் மட்டும் ஊடல் காட்டி உடனே கலங்கினாள்; ஏனெனில், என்னை விட அவளே தழுவிக்கொள்வதில் அதிக அவசரம் கொண்டிருந்தாள்.
ai.explanation: The heroine attempts to feign anger (sulk) to playfully delay their union, but she can only manage to show it through her eyes. She immediately loses her resolve and becomes confused because her own desire to embrace her lover is far greater than his. Her intense eagerness (vituppu) to embrace overcomes her attempt at sulking (tuni). This couplet beautifully captures the conflict between a lover's desire to play-act anger and her overwhelming passion that defeats her own game.
